leads.title: Earthen mound complexes in the Lower Mississippi Valley
leads.where: Watson Brake and other sites, Louisiana
leads.why: Hunter-gatherers laid out planned mound groups two thousand years before Poverty Point, beginning the long tradition of earthen monuments in eastern North America.
leads.verify: Dating and layout of the Middle Archaic mounds (Watson Brake, Frenchman's Bend, the Louisiana State University mounds) and whether a continuous tradition links them to Poverty Point (c. 1700 BCE) and to later Woodland and Mississippian mound building.

leads.title: Monumental platforms and pyramids in Formative Mesoamerica
leads.where: Gulf Coast and Maya lowlands, Mexico and Guatemala
leads.why: Raised plazas and pyramids became the core of every later Mesoamerican centre, from La Venta to Teotihuacan and Tenochtitlan.
leads.verify: The earliest large works and their dates: the San Lorenzo plateau, the great platform of Aguada Fenix (c. 1000 to 800 BCE), the La Venta pyramid, early Maya E-groups. The Maya corbelled vault and burnt-lime stucco belong to this tradition and may merit their own records.

leads.title: Stone temple platforms in East Polynesia
leads.where: Society Islands, Rapa Nui, Hawaiian and Marquesas Islands
leads.why: Marae, ahu and heiau organised ritual and chiefly power on islands across a third of the Pacific, and on Rapa Nui carried the moai.
leads.verify: Dated sequences for the earliest marae and ahu (uranium-thorium coral dates from Mo'orea, radiocarbon from Rapa Nui and Hawai'i), how the forms relate across islands, and the methods of moving and raising the stone.

leads.title: Steel-skeleton tall buildings in Chicago
leads.why: The frame, with the elevator, produced the skyscraper and the high-rise city, and framed construction became the norm for large buildings everywhere.
leads.verify: How far the Home Insurance Building (1885) was truly frame-carried, and the first fully steel-framed buildings (1889 to 1890). The line behind it: the cast-iron arch at Coalbrookdale (1779), the iron-framed Ditherington flax mill (1797), the Crystal Palace and French iron framing. Structural iron in Britain may merit its own record.

leads.title: Water-storage dams in the Early Bronze Age Levant and Egypt
leads.why: Stored floodwater let a town live in the basalt desert; dam building continued in the region through Marib and the Nabataean and Roman works.
leads.verify: Dating and design of the Jawa reservoirs and dams and of the Sadd el-Kafara in Egypt (which failed), and whether later Near Eastern dam building descends from them. Dams in Mesoamerica (the Purron dam, Tehuacan valley, from c. 750 BCE) and in South Asia are separate origins.

leads.title: Aqueduct water supply in the Aztec Basin of Mexico
leads.where: Tenochtitlan and Texcoco, Basin of Mexico
leads.why: Twin-channel aqueducts brought spring water across the lake to an island city of some two hundred thousand, alongside dikes that kept salt water from the fresh.
leads.verify: Dates and builders of the Chapultepec aqueducts and of Nezahualcoyotl's dike (1449) and the Tetzcotzinco works, from sixteenth-century sources and archaeology. Earlier Mesoamerican water channels (Palenque, Teotihuacan, Monte Alban) set the background. The existing record for this concept is a Roman instance; a first-known record (Assyrian Jerwan, c. 690 BCE) is still missing.

concepts.name: Aqueduct
concepts.summary: A built channel that carries water by gravity over long distances to supply a settlement or works.

concepts.name: Dam
concepts.summary: A barrier built across a watercourse to store water or turn it aside.

concepts.name: Monumental construction
concepts.summary: Building works far larger than any dwelling, by organised communal labour, for ceremony, burial or display.

concepts.name: Skeleton-frame tall building
concepts.summary: Carrying a building's whole weight on an internal frame of metal columns and beams, so that walls become a light skin and height is no longer limited by masonry.
